scores.notes: The piece leans so hard on what it can't prove, repeating the same caveats and the 2→9→1 page counts in nearly every section, that the strong contrast between the second and third rewrites gets diluted. It also invents claims the author never made, such as pages being 'customer evidence' and the 'noise from a new system settling in' rationale.

The post says the 40,000 rows were lost in the second incident and that `--rename-map` answers the rename questions ahead of time; the author answers support neither claim, and there is no command example or sample output to show how tidepool works.

The material is strong, but the piece leans on repeated not-X-but-Y turns and tidy one-line section closers, and its ending lesson ('put the lunch on the calendar the day you cancel') feels pre-packaged rather than earned.

The angle is the stock small-room plant post, 'pick the right plants for your light,' and the author's sharpest details, the landlord's remark and the per-plant watering log, are reported flatly instead of carrying the piece.

The piece repeats the same three numbers four or five times and stacks on meta-commentary ('its shortness is the point', 'I don't think that's a coincidence', the 'common version of this post' setup), so a thin story gets padded to essay length when it needs more scene detail.

The piece is padded: it repeats the 6am call, the 'nicer diagram' line and the test several times, and it hedges and recaps at length ('I'll let the number speak for itself', the arc summary, the three 'Not...' lines), which dilutes a strong, honest core.

The middle section explains a point HN readers already accept (renames are ambiguous) and never shows the actual prompt or a sample `--rename-map` file, so it leans on story instead of showing the tool.

The post needs the real install and diff commands, and their placeholders leave it unpostable. Repeating the 40,000-rows hook in the closing line, plus a neat 'Now it asks.' ending, reads like a pitch rather than a Show HN first comment.

The piece leans heavily on disclaimers like 「我說不準」「老實說」 and on lines that just restate the author's answers, so the 'who pays the cost' angle feels thin. The closing three-item list and the not-X-but-Y framing also feel formulaic.

The author can't remember any concrete scene, so the piece fills the gap with talk about uncertainty. It repeats the two quotes and says 'I don't know' several times, and the one emotional idea, that people only notice the meeting once it's gone, is stated rather than shown.

The piece lists every author fact as a tidy how-to, with no felt moment or specific failure story, and it invents details to fill the gaps: the landlord pausing at the door, the rod needing no drilled holes, and no longer having to replace pots.
The piece leans on stock not-X-but-Y lines ('不是植物說了算，是你的窗說了算', '不再問…改問…'), adds a closing line that restates the ending, and never shows a single specific plant moment, so it reads like a template.

The piece keeps announcing what it doesn't remember (cause, fixer, the realization moment, the trigger) and those disclaimers take up whole paragraphs, while tidy closers like 'The diagram never had to answer that call' and the not-X-but-Y lesson sound written to a formula.

The piece invents two details: that the 40,000 rows were lost 'the second time', and that 'the SQL looked fine and ran cleanly'. Neither appears in the author's answers, and the author said they don't know why their earlier process missed the rename.

The piece over-explains its own thesis. It restates the 'one meeting did two jobs' point in several sections, and the tidy three-bullet advice list and moralizing one-line closers weaken the specific material from Ada and 小周.

The window-as-selector angle is set up well but stops early: the body goes back to a checklist of the author's facts, and it adds details the author never gave, such as buying ferns because they looked nice, plants crowded near the window, and asking questions in a shop.

The post keeps saying what it can't say: the disclaimers about the unknown 9-page breakdown and the unattributed Ohio triple charge go on too long, and repeated self-justifying passages ('I'm not going to make one up', 'That's the point') dull a strong confession.

The post never shows the rename prompt, a command or sample output, so HN readers learn the premise but not what using tidepool is like. The author couldn't supply these details, but the post doesn't say that, and the three CI questions read like a stock list.

The piece pads thin material with repeated statistic recaps (2→9, 11 weeks, and 3 weeks restated four or five times), repeated 'I can't remember' hedges, and stacked rule-of-three 'Not X. Not Y. Not Z.' frames, so it reads long and circular.

The middle section explains the rename-versus-drop ambiguity, which HN readers already know, using neat contrast lines ("You know what you meant. The diff doesn't."), while the concrete 40,000-row incident gets only one sentence.

The angle repeats the author's own conclusion instead of finding a sharper one, and the piece keeps saying it doesn't remember things ('記不清' comes up three times). Those repeated disclaimers, plus several not-X-but-Y frames and short one-line closers, make the second half feel padded.

The piece mostly restates the author's facts in order with a generic tip at the end. There is no sensory detail or specific moment, such as what a dying fern looked like or how the west sun felt in the room. The closer, "先選對植物，比學再多照顧技巧都有用", reads like a stock aphorism.
